statement: Let $\alpha$ be a root of $x^{3}-3x+1=0$. Show that $\alpha^{2}-2$ is also a root of this equation.
solution: Since $\alpha^{3}-3\alpha+1=0$ we have $\alpha^{3}=3\alpha-1$. Let $\beta=\alpha^{2}-2$. Then $\alpha^{4}=\alpha\cdot\alpha^{3}=\alpha(3\alpha-1)=3\alpha^{2}-\alpha$ and $\alpha^{6}=(\alpha^{3})^{2}=(3\alpha-1)^{2}=9\alpha^{2}-6\alpha+1$. Now $\beta^{3}=(\alpha^{2}-2)^{3}=\alpha^{6}-6\alpha^{4}+12\alpha^{2}-8 =(9\alpha^{2}-6\alpha+1)-6(3\alpha^{2}-\alpha)+12\alpha^{2}-8=3\alpha^{2}-7$. Hence $\beta^{3}-3\beta+1=(3\alpha^{2}-7)-3(\alpha^{2}-2)+1=0$, so $\beta$ is a root.
hints: Use $\alpha^{3}=3\alpha-1$ to reduce higher powers of $\alpha$.
Compute $(\alpha^{2}-2)^{3}$ and simplify using the relation.
